idiom_name: virtual accept(Visitor&) with one visit(const ConcreteElement&) overload per node type
implementation_notes: The textbook C++ form: Element declares virtual accept(Visitor&) and each concrete element's override is a one-liner calling v.visit(*this), so overload resolution on the static type of *this selects the right visit() member - that is the second dispatch, and it is why pure virtual visit overloads give compile-time completeness. It works for hierarchies that must stay open to new subclasses and for ABI-stable plugin interfaces, and it is the only form that supports multiple simultaneous element hierarchies (visit(const A&, const B&) gives multi-method dispatch). The price is the pattern's own: a new element type edits the visitor interface and every visitor, and the two hierarchies include each other, so large ASTs usually pair it with the acyclic variant or forward declarations.
pitfalls: Implementing accept() in the base class only: *this is then Shape&, overload resolution picks the wrong (or no) visit overload, and the double dispatch silently degrades into type tests.
Omitting the virtual destructor on the element base: deleting through the base pointer is undefined behaviour, and element hierarchies are usually heap-owned.
Mutating or reallocating elements while a visitor holds references - visiting is not a mutation API; collect changes and apply them after the walk.
The mutually dependent headers (visitor needs element declarations, elements need the visitor) make layering and build times fragile; forward-declare where possible.

variants.name: std::variant + std::visit with an overload set (value-based visiting)
variants.idiom_name: std::visit(overloaded{...}, value) over a closed std::variant
variants.implementation_notes: The C++17 value alternative: model the closed set of shapes as std::variant and write each operation as an overload set of lambdas (the overload/overloaded helper inherits their operator() and exposes them with using Ts::operator()...); std::visit dispatches on the active alternative and the program does not compile if one is unhandled. It inverts the classic trade cleanly - the type set is closed in the variant declaration while adding an operation needs no edit anywhere - and it needs no heap and no vtable when variants hold values. Choose it for sum types you own; keep the classic virtual form when the hierarchy must stay open to new subclasses, when elements live behind a stable plugin ABI, or when the same visitor must visit two hierarchies at once.
pitfalls: An overload set with implicit conversions compiles even when an alternative is missing (a lambda taking double swallows int); add a template operator() with static_assert(always_false_v<T>) or a C++20 consteval catch-all to turn that back into a compile error.
Exhaustiveness only holds for non-generic lambdas: one auto&& arm silently absorbs every unhandled alternative.
std::visit with many alternatives compiles to a jump table or a nested switch; for large variants a manual dispatch on the discriminant index can be faster and keeps binary size down.
Converting a polymorphic hierarchy to a variant is a redesign, not a refactor: recursive variants need indirection (Box/unique_ptr) and values are copied where pointers used to be.
